title: Who changed it, who fought it and who changed it back
lede: Titles are as given in the press at the time. Later careers are left out where we have no source.

people.name: Roberto C. Goizueta
people.role: Chairman and CEO, The Coca-Cola Company
people.text: Introduced the new formula on April 23, 1985 and announced the return of the old one in July.[^8][^16] A reader addressed a letter to “Chief Dodo, The Coca-Cola Company,” and it was delivered.[^1]
people.later: At a tenth-anniversary event in 1995 he called the decision a prime example of “taking intelligent risks.”[^1]

people.name: Donald R. Keough
people.text: Toasted the new drink at Lincoln Center and gave the speech that took it back.[^16][^27] At the 1986 centennial, aged 59, he said: “It all kind of worked out.”[^9]
people.later: Still on Coca-Cola’s board in 2005.[^18] Fortune reported his death in February 2015.[^28]

people.name: Brian Dyson
people.text: The executive who gave the numbers in June 1985: 1,500 calls a day, 110 million triers, an 18-month plan.[^5]

people.name: Sergio Zyman
people.text: Named by a 2005 retrospective among the “top brass” who decided to concede.[^18]

people.name: Gay Mullins
people.role: Founder, Old Cola Drinkers of America
people.text: A Seattle retiree who set up a complaint hotline, claimed 100,000 members and sued. He said he spent about $100,000.[^6][^7][^27] In a taste test he could not pick out the drink he was fighting for.[^7]
people.later: Mother Jones, drawing on Thomas Oliver’s 1986 book, reports that he later asked Coca-Cola for $200,000 for an endorsement and was turned down.[^27]

people.name: Roger Enrico
people.text: Signed the advertisement that said “the other guy just blinked.”[^24]

people.name: Harold Burson
people.text: Advised the company to be contrite, though by the same account he too had believed in the new drink.[^18]

people.name: Jesse Meyers
people.text: The trade source for the share figures of 1985. He called the reversal “absolutely” the result of the negative reaction.[^6]
